pronunciation.approximation: BRAH-ghi — a short open 'ah', and the g softening between vowels to a light voiced fricative, like a gentle 'gh'; stress falls on the first syllable.
pronunciation.note: Old Norse Bragi is bound to the poetic noun bragr, which carries two senses at once: 'poetry' and 'foremost, chief, the best' (Cleasby–Vigfusson, s.v. bragr). Snorri derives the noun from the god — from Bragi's name bragr is called, and from it a man or woman of eloquence is a bragr-maðr or bragr-kona — while modern etymologists argue over which direction the derivation truly runs. The normalized Old Norse form is plain ASCII: no diacritic, no thorn or eth, nothing for the ASCII alphabet to lose. Tier-2 by the mechanical rule — a statement about orthography, never about the god Grímnismál calls the best of skalds.

domains.title: Poetry, Eloquence
domains.subtitle: The Skald Among the Gods
domains.lead: Bragi is the god the North made out of its own craft: the god of poetry and of the well-turned word, husband of Iðunn, the voice Snorri seats at the centre of every divine feast — the skald who narrates the myths to Ægir in the Prose Edda's own frame, and the god Óðinn sends out to greet dead kings at the door of Valhǫll.

cards.name: The Mead of Poetry
cards.desc: The blood-and-honey mead brewed from wise Kvasir, hoarded by Suttungr and stolen by Óðinn — the myth of poetry's origin that Bragi himself narrates in Skáldskaparmál.

cards.name: The Bragarfull
cards.desc: The 'foremost cup' drained with binding vows at the great feasts — the toast that kept the god's word for 'foremost' at the drinking-table long after conversion.

cards.name: The Long Beard
cards.desc: Skegg-Bragi: Skáldskaparmál's kenning calls him the long-bearded god — the beard as the old skald's visible mark of office.

cards.name: The King's Welcome
cards.desc: The voice at Valhǫll's door: in Hákonarmál Óðinn sends Bragi and Hermóðr out to greet the dead king Hákon the Good as he comes to the hall.

symbols.name: The mead of poetry
symbols.meaning: Poetry as a liquid that can be brewed, stolen, and shared — inspiration made drinkable

symbols.name: The bragarfull
symbols.meaning: The foremost cup of the vow-toast — the spoken word made binding over drink

symbols.name: The long beard
symbols.meaning: Snorri's kenning for the god — age, memory, and the skald's authority worn on the face

symbols.name: The bench in Ægir's hall
symbols.meaning: The storyteller's seat at the feast — eloquence as a hospitality the gods themselves require

symbols.name: The greeting of dead kings
symbols.meaning: The word that meets greatness at death's door — praise as the North's answer to mortality

mythology.lead: Bragi acts in almost nothing and speaks in everything. His dossier is a voice: the catalogue portrait in Gylfaginning, the storytelling frame of Skáldskaparmál, the first sharp answer to Loki in Lokasenna, and the welcome spoken over dead kings in the court poems. The tradition made the god of poetry out of the thing poetry does.

myths.title: The Best of Skalds
myths.text: Snorri's catalogue of the Æsir fixes the portrait the whole tradition repeats: one of the gods is called Bragi; he is renowned for wisdom and most of all for eloquence and skill with words, and he knows more about poetry than any other. From his name, Snorri says, bragr is called — the word means both poetry and the foremost of anything — and from it a man or woman who surpasses others in eloquence is called a bragr-maðr or bragr-kona. His wife is Iðunn. Grímnismál's litany of the world's best things seals the verdict in verse: Bragi is best of skalds, as Sleipnir is best of horses and Bifrǫst of bridges.

myths.title: The Gods' Own Storyteller
myths.text: The Prose Edda's second half is built around Bragi's voice. When Ægir, the sea-god skilled in magic, came to a feast in Ásgarðr, he was seated beside Bragi, and they drank and talked — and the myths Bragi tells him are the ones the book exists to record: how the Æsir and Vanir spat their truce into a vat and made Kvasir, wisest of beings; how the dwarfs Fjalarr and Galarr killed him and brewed his blood with honey into the mead that makes a skald of whoever drinks; how the mead passed to the giant Suttungr and how Óðinn, as Bǫlverkr, lay three nights with Gunnlǫð and drained Óðrerir in three gulps. Bragi also tells Ægir how the giant Þjazi took the shape of an eagle and carried off his own wife Iðunn and her apples of youth, and how Loki won her back. When Skáldskaparmál later asks how Bragi himself shall be kennt, the answer is the god's whole identity in one line: husband of Iðunn, first maker of poetry, the long-bearded god, and son of Óðinn.

myths.title: The First Answer in Ægir's Hall
myths.text: When Loki forced his way into Ægir's feast uninvited and demanded a place at the drinking, Bragi was the first of the Æsir to refuse him: the gods, he said, know whom they will have at their high feast, and Loki is not one. Loki invoked Óðinn's old oath of blood-brotherhood and won his seat — and then began the flyting the poem is named for. To Bragi he threw the insult that stings a skald most: that the god of the word was the most cowardly of the Æsir in war, shyest of the bow-shot when fighting came. Bragi answered that if they stood outside the hall he would carry Loki's head in his hand — and then it was Iðunn, his wife, who did the true eloquent work of the scene, begging Bragi not to bandy words with Loki in Ægir's hall and calming the quarrel before it ran further. The poem keeps Bragi exactly where the tradition always keeps him: at the bench, in the war of words.

myths.title: The Greeter of Dead Kings
myths.text: The court poets gave Bragi his most solemn office. In Eyvindr skáldaspillir's Hákonarmál, composed for the funeral of King Hákon the Good around 961, Óðinn looks out as the slain king approaches Valhǫll with his host and speaks the order the North remembered: 'Hermóðr and Bragi, go to meet the king — a king who seems mighty is coming to the hall.' In the anonymous Eiríksmál, woven for Eiríkr Bloodaxe, it is Bragi who speaks with Óðinn inside the hall: he asks why the Allfather robbed Eiríkr of victory when the king seemed to him the bravest, and Óðinn answers with the sentence that explains all such losses — the grey wolf gapes ever at the dwellings of the gods. The god of poetry is the one who must ask why the brave die, and the one sent out to welcome them home.

myths.title: Bragi Boddason and the God-Making Poet
myths.text: History keeps a second Bragi, and the two have never been fully separated. Bragi Boddason the Old, a Norwegian skald of the ninth century, is the earliest skald whose name and verse both survive: his Ragnarsdrápa, a shield-poem of painted myths, is quoted stanza by stanza in Skáldskaparmál, and Skáldatal counts him among the skalds of Ragnarr loðbrók. Since the nineteenth century scholars have asked whether the god is the deified poet — a great court skald promoted after death into the pantheon he served — and the handbooks register the theory without settling it. Simek notes the other, colder possibility: that the divine Bragi may be a late literary personification of bragr, poetry itself, with no old cult behind him at all. Between the poet made god and the god made out of a noun, the sources leave the question honestly open.

lore.syncretism: Bragi invites comparisons, and the honest ones are typological, not genealogical. The Irish Ogma of the Tuatha Dé Danann — champion of eloquence, credited with the Ogham script — is his closest structural kin in the neighbouring tradition: two Indo-European cultures that each enthroned the well-spoken word among their gods, with no borrowing argued or needed. The Greek comparison is weaker: Bragi is no Apollo, for he neither leads a choir nor prophesies, and the North already gave the mead of poetry's conquest to Óðinn. What Bragi has that the Greeks never made into a god is the skald's office itself — praise as a profession, memory as a wage, the poem as the contract between a king and his fame. The deepest syncretic question is internal: whether Bragi is a personification of bragr raised to godhood, or the euhemerized Bragi Boddason absorbed into his own subject matter. Either way, he is the most Germanic of answers to the question of where poetry lives: it lives at the feast, with a name that means 'foremost'.
lore.culturalLegacy: Bragi never left the North's language. Bragr remained the Old Norse word for poetry itself; the bragr-maðr and bragr-kona — the man or woman of surpassing eloquence — kept his name in everyday compliment; and the bragarfull, the foremost cup of the vow-toast that Ynglinga saga sets at the great inheritance feasts, carried the word into the drinking customs of medieval Scandinavia and, revived, into the sumbel of modern Heathen practice, where Bragi is still hailed as the patron of poets before the boasting rounds begin. The name lives on as a Scandinavian given name — Bragi in Iceland, Brage in Norway and Sweden — and Norway's premier literary award, the Brage Prize, has borne it since 1992. The white-bearded Bragi with a harp who appears in nineteenth-century Scandinavian painting and sculpture is a Romantic addition: the Eddas give him no instrument, only the voice — which was, of course, the whole point.
lore.extendedMeditation: Bragi is the god a culture of oral memory had to invent. In a world without archives, the skald was the archive: the king's deeds, the clan's honour, the boundary between being remembered and being nothing all ran through one trained voice at the feast. The North looked at that voice and saw a god in it — and then, characteristically, put the god to work at the door of the dead, because the only immortality the Edda truly promises is the welcome spoken over you when you arrive. Óðinn wins the mead; Bragi pours it. That division of labour is the deepest thing the tradition says about poetry: inspiration is theft and ordeal, but eloquence is hospitality — the craft of receiving greatness and giving it words. The god whose name means 'foremost' is the one who stands where the living greet the dead and finds the sentence both can bear.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Bragi — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛒᚱᛅᚴᛁ (b-r-a-k-i, the ᚴ rune writing g as well as k). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: bragi.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Bragi is a textual god: no runestone invokes him, no votive deposit names him, and the place-name record offers no secure theophoric site — the silence that leads Simek and Lindow to weigh him as a late literary personification rather than an old cult figure. The runic corpus does know the name, but only as an ordinary human anthroponym: Bragi is well attested as a Viking-Age man's name in Scandinavian inscriptions, which is precisely the problem for cult-hunters, since none of the carvings can be tied to the god. The witnesses are therefore the manuscripts. Lokasenna and Grímnismál survive in the thirteenth-century Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda; Gylfaginning and the Skáldskaparmál frame in the Codex Regius and sister manuscripts of the Prose Edda, with Skáldatal in the Uppsala codex; Hákonarmál rides inside the Heimskringla tradition and Eiríksmál inside Fagrskinna. The famous image of Bragi as an old harper belongs to nineteenth-century art, not to the material record: no medieval carving, pendant, or picture stone shows him.
